CURRIE (North Simcoe)moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 107) to amend the Adulteration Act.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER Explain.

The Bill first does away with the necessity of a deposit of money by the complainant in the case of goods being sold that are adulterated. The Adulteration Act provides that if anyone enters a complaint he must deposit with the officer sufficient money to cover the cost of purchasing a sample, and secondly, sufficient money to cover the cost of an analysis. _ I consider this a hardship on the public when parliament provides large sums of money for these officers and when, acording to the Auditor General's report, large sums are spent annually in purchasing samples for analysis.
The second clause is intended to simplify the prosecution. We have no prosecutions to speak of under this Act because the Act provides that the informant must deposit $25 with the officer as a guarantee of the costs of the prosecution; or, in other words, if anyone wishes to enforce this public Act he must first deposit $25 with the official. The Adulteration Act also provides that the complainant or informant shall receive a portion of the fine. The second clause of this Bill does away with this provision altogether and simply states that the officer shall prosecute in the same manner as under any other Act so that anyone may lay an information without making a deposit. Thus the law would be carried out and the offender fined but the informant would not receive a portion of the fine. Under this system there would be no inducement for anyone to become an informer beyond the desire to carry out the provisions of the Act. When this matter was under discussion in the House it was shown that whilst a great number of analyses had been made by the department, hardly any prosecutions had been made and if a firm or person were guilty of adulterating goods the only punishment suffered was the fact of their having sold adulterated goods was published in the pamphlets issued from time to time by the government. I think the time has come when the same course should be pursued in the enforcement of this Act as of any other Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
LEWIS (West Huron) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 108) intituled the Daylight Saving Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Explain.

I can best explain the provisions of this Act by, for two or three minutes, explaining the position of time in Great Britain and in Canada. On June 15. 1881, Mr. Sandford Fleming civil engineer, now Sir Sandford Fleming, made a report, which was really an essay, as to the time system then in use in Canada. We were then using the system which had been in vogue from time immemorial. On the 17th of June, 1882, Sir Sandford Fleming as chairman of the committee appointed for the purpose of looking into the question recommended a standard system of time for different parts of the country instead of the existing time system which changed with each degree of latitude, and in 1883 our present system was adopted in Canada. We have now in Canada four systems of time, namely, the eastern system, the central system, the mountain system, the Pacific system, not including the Atlantic system or the Yukon system, with regard to which there is special legislation in the Yukon territory. In the United K; igiom they have always been using mean time, namely Greenwich time or Dublin time. Some two or three years ago a gentleman named William Willets, who had been accustomed to early rising, began to realize that most of the people of England were lying in bed during the best hours of the day, that the best part of the sun-lit day was lost to the people and that the hours of recreation for workingmen were in twilight and dark when they might just as well be in the hours of daylight. Mr. Willets found that this condition of things affected adversely, more particularly the working men, the artizans, the agriculturalists, and the youth of the land. He agitated his scheme with the result that in March, 1908, the British parliament appointed a commission of nine members to investigate the subject and evidence was taken , the report of which may be found in the library. There was a majority report brought in by eight members of that commission and a minority report by one. The majority report contained this recommendation:.
The Select Committee to whom the Daylight Saving Bill was referred, have agreed to the following special report:-
1.	That the committee have met and considered the said Bill, and have examined numerous witnesses, records and papers and have directed the said Bill to he reported to the House with amendments.
2.	And the committee find that the Bill proposes the adoption of a local time in advance of Greenwich mean time in the case of Great Britain, and in advance of Dublin mean time

in the case of Ireland, during the summer months, viz.:	from April to September in
each year, with the object of promoting the earlier and more extended use and enjoyment of daylight during those months. And that such object is desirable and would benefit the community if it can be generally attained, and that the weight of the evidence submitted to the committee agrees with and supports this view, though there was divergence of opinion as to the best mode of accomplishing it.
The effect of the proposals of the Bill would be:-
(1)	To move the usual hours of work and
leisure nearer to sunrise.	_
(2)	To promote the greater use of daylight for recreative purposes of all kinds.
(3)	To benefit the physique, general health and ivelfare of all classes of the community.
(4)	To reduce the industrial, commercial and. domestic expenditure on artificial light.
A Bill founded on this report was introduced in the Imperial House of Commons and passed through its second reading last session. This year a similar Bill was introduced, read a second time, and submitted to a special committee for a report. The Bill which I propose submitting to the House is drafted on the same lines as the English Bill so far as the conditions in Canada will admit and is as follows:
An Act respecting the system of time now in
use in Canada.
This Act shall be known as the Daylight Saving Bill.
Whereas, the adoption of a local time in Canada in advance of the standard time now in use there during the summer months for the object of promoting the earlier and more extended use and enjoyment of daylight during said period is desirable.
Therefore, His Majesty by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
1.	From two o'clock in the morning of the last day of April in each year in Canada until two o'clock in the morning of the last day in October in each year in Canada the local time shall be one hour in advance of the standard time as now in use in Canada.
2.	The time hereby established shall be known as local time in Canada, and whenever any period of time is mentioned in any Act of parliament, deed, or other legal instrument, the time mentioned or referred to shall, unless it is otherwise specifically stated, be held in the case of Canada to be local time as prescribed by this Act.
3.	Greenwich mean time as used for the purposes of astronomy and navigation shall not be affected by this Act.
4.	This Act shall' apply to the Dominion of Canada, save and except the Yukon Territory, and may be cited as the Daylight Saving Act, and shall not come into force until one year from the date of passing of same.
I might state to the House that a number of localities in Canada have attempted to adopt some such system as is here outlined, but their efforts have not been successful as they could not legally alter the standard

time. The city of Nelson in British Columbia has been much agitated over the question for the last two or three months, and in Fort William and Port Arthur an unsuccessful attempt was made to deal with it. I would point out that after the first change is made there would be really no inconvenience to the people of Canada, and I feel they would soon become used to and highly pleased with the system which I propose. In Canada on April 30 the sun rises at 11 minutes past 5 o'clock and sets at 18 minutes past 7 o'clock; on October 31 the sun rises at 52 minutes past six o'clock and sets at 11 minutes past five o'clock. These are the dates set in the proposed Bill. I trust that Canada will not be backward in this movement, and I would ask the government to appoint a committee to investigate and to confer with the authorities in England, the United States, Australia and New Zealand, the latter countries having started legislation on these lines. I believe that if my idea is carried into legislation it will he conducive to the health and wealth of the labouring men, of the workingmen, and of the farmers of Canada.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

If there is any one rule well understood, it is that before granting supplies grievances must be redressed, and this is a grievance the opposition have to contend with.

My idea in calling the attention of the hon. member to the point is very evident: We are about to go into Supply, and, as the matter under discussion is before the Committee of Supply, I thought it would be better to know how the House intends to proceed. Would my hon. friend pardon me? I admit that that was a mis-

take. The name was given to me by one of my officials.

I would like to ask the minister if tenders have been called, and, if so, the names of the tenderers and the amount of each tender.
The work is under contract to F. S. Macdonald, of Souris, P.E.I., and the contract price is $12,995.

I would like to have the name and the amount of each tender?

The primary thing for a minister to have, when he is asked for the name of the successful tenderer, is the names of the other tenderers, and the amounts of their tenders. I would ask the Minister of Public Works if this is sometimes called the Panmure wharf?

That is where Panmure Island is. Although the wharf was built two years ago, the right of way to it has not yet been opened to the public. I would like the minister to have that done as soon as possible.

The contract for this work has just been let. It has been pressed on the attention of the department for a good many years. Tignish is a very important point, particularly as a harbour of refuge for fishermen. I may say that there have been protection works built at Tignish, but they are not adequate to the protection of the harbour, and the present works include the extension of the northern and southern breakwater, 650 feet and 620 feet respectively, and the construction of a breastwork to extend 400 feet from either end of the breakwaters. Do public tenders mean public advertisement in the newspapers?
Yes.

I have not the number here, but at least a dozen.

I am inclined to think so. I can name one at any rate.

I would not care to name it.

To purchase ereosoted timber for worts in the maritime provinces generally, $20,000.
What is the system followed ?

The resident engineers in the lower provinces, in making provision for repairs to wharfs, where the teredo is likely to prove harmful to ordinary timber, estimate for ereosoted timber. That is obtained in the south. We have no creo-soting works in Eastern Canada. The wood is southern pine, and it is treated at Norfolk, Virginia. There are only two concerns engaged in the work.	*
What kind of a contract do you make P
We do not ask for public tenders but obtain prices and take the lowest provided the timber passes a certain test. We require that it shall pass the test of our inspector.
How do you test it?
I am not aware of the details, but there is a regular mode of testing the quantity of creosote which is forced into the timber.
Why not have the timber ereosoted in Canada P

It would require an expenditure of a quarter of a million dollars
to establish a plant.

I understand there are
two methods-one by forcing the creosote into the wood by pressure and the other by boiling the wood in creosote.
The boiling is of no use. The oil must be forced in by pressure. The sap has to be drawn out by putting the timber in a vacum, and then the oil of creosote takes the place of the sap.
What extra cost does this creosoting entail ?
It trebles the cost, but more than trebles the life of the timber.
Is the timber bought by the department direct ?
No, through agents. The agents are Mr. Kirk of Nova Scotia and Mr. Pell of St. John.
What price was paid last year ?
I think about $65 per 1000 feet. It depends on the length of the sticks. Long sticks would be worth more.

How much was bought
last year ?

Up to the 1st of February, we bought $9,711 worth.
Naufrage pond, Prince Edward Island- protecting entrance channel, $11,500.

I have the information which my hon. friend from Kings county (Mr. Fraser) desired. The parties tendering were: F. S. Macdonald, Souris, Prince Edward Island, $12,995; R. N. Cox, Morell, Prince Edward Island, $13,800; Kimbell, Coffin, Calien McCarthy, H. D. McEwen, $14,925. The contract was given to F S. Macdonald at $12,995.

In Bonaventure.

It is being prepared as rapidly as possible.
Mr. Foster. It is hardly in order to take up the items to be included in that return until the return has been brought down.

There is a great deal of work about the return, and it cannot be ready for two weeks. I do not think the return would in any way affect the passing of these items. This is a revote, to complete the work.

Yes.
Not in reference particularly to this item, but generally, could the minister tell us how he proceeds when he undertakes a construction like this by day's work? What is the process?

The process is to instruct the resident engineer to proceed with the work by day's labour. He is instructed to confer with the member for the county supporting the government as to the names of competent foremen, to begin with, to take charge of the work, and also to purchase material at the lowest price.
From whom?
He is to use his judgment.
Whom does he consult as to that?
He has no instructions on that point.
What is the practice?
I am not able to say. I suppose that in this also he would consult the member supporting the government.	-
What price does he pay for labour?
The ordinary price paid in the neighbourhood.
And as to material?
He buys that at fair market prices.
Who buys it?
The resident engineer.
From whom does he buy?
From dealers.
Who keeps the pay-roll?
The resident engineer.
Can the resident engineer whose time is not entirely devoted to one of these little works, keep the weekly pay-roll?
Oh, no, the foreman must do that. The foreman certifies to the resident engineer, and the resident engineer certifies to the chief engineer.
Does the engineer receive instructions to buy at the lowest prices?
Yes.
Always?
Always.
Very often they do not do it.
I am very sorry to hear that.

Now, as I brought this matter up, I may be permitted a remark. We have got a lot of information in a very short space of time. The system is a lovely system in theory-and it can be even more lovely in practice. Shorn of all verbiage, what does this mean? It means that the work, from beginning to end, is in the hands of the representative of the county supporting the government and is used for his party benefit, to go no further. When the work is decided upon, the resident engineer is told to go on and do the work by day labour. He applies first-and last and always-to the member who represents the county. He needs foremen to supervise the labouring men; the member for the county appoints them. He needs material for the work; the member for the county tells him where to go to get it. He needs to know the prices to pay for them; he consults the member of the county as to the prices.
No.
The pay-rolls are kept by the nominee of the member for the county, that is by the member for the county himself.
Or the defeated government candidate.

Yes, or the unsuccessful candidate in the interests of the government. It all inures to the party benefit, either to the member supporting the government or to the defeated candidate who wishes, next time, to be elected to support the government. These facts are sufficient condemnation of the system. The minister's power is absolutely nil, so far as any real effectiveness is concerned. No independent supervision is given over the matter, with the exception of what the resident engineer may give and he is not independent. The first thing he is told to do is to consult the member representing the county, if he is in favour of the government. Now under that svstem any one can understand wliat is going on in the public works of this country in the expenditure of millions of dollars, a very considerable portion of

which is done by day's work. It seems to me that this is a very bad system, both for the government and for the political life of the country.

The remarks of the hon. member for North Toronto would certainly apply where the pier is a large work involving a large amount of money. But I lay it down as a general principle that when the amount to be expended is less than $5,000, it is better not to call for tenders. For instance, in the counties of Bon-aventure and Gasp6 several small works have been going on for the last ten or fifteen years. Now take a small pier which is being built, to cost less than $5,000; would it be wise on the part of the government to call for tenders over all portions of Canada, or the whole district of Quebec, for instance, for the construction of that work? We would have to expend considerable money in advertisements, we know that newspapers are not paid by prayers, and we would have to spend a large amount of money in notices, advertisements and so on. Now take the county of Gaspe where this particular work is being done. The resident engineer of course is supposed to be an honest man, he belongs to a profession which naturally makes of him an honest man. He has to supervise the work for which a certain sum of money has been voted by parliament. Well, what interest would the resident engineer have in spending that money in an unwise manner? Would he take the advice of any one, and pay for timber a higher price than the market value? All accounts have to come back to the Public Works Department, where they are carefully checked by Mr. Kingston, I believe, an expert, who has been there many years. I know as a matter of fact, having had some experience with works of this kind in that district, that accounts have been checked and payment has been refused when the price appeared to be above the market price. So we can take it for granted that the market price is the one paid by the Department of Public Works. As regards paying the men- well, I am always speaking for the district of Gaspe. I have received letter after letter from my electors complaining that they had not been paid what they were entitled to. There is in every contract a clause inserted by the Department of Labour called the fair wage clause, which governs the payment of wages, so that in each district only the market price is paid for labour. This is known and adopted in the particular district. So there is no possibility, unless the resident engineer is a thief, of the department being swindled by people who are employed on those works. The acounts for the timber, the accounts for the stone, the accounts for labour, are all checked by

Mr. Kingston, the chief accountant of the Public Works Department, and I do not see : how the department can be swindled at all. My hon. friend says it is all a piece of partisanship, that only friends of the government are employed. Well, let me say this to my hon. friend: The county of GaspS has elected me by acclamation many times, or by large majorities, since 1896, and it would be folly on my part to say to the resident engineer: You will employ only so and so. He must not make any difference, he must employ his men irrespective of politics.
Let us argue this question out in a common sense way.
How was it about fifteen years ago?

That doesn't amount to anything it all. We are trying now to see whether this is a good way to spend the people's money. What uoes the present system amount to? In the first place, the member representing the county, if he supports the government, obtains the work, and what is the next thing he does? There is a work to be carried on by the day's labour system as it has been portrayed by the minister. He goes down to his constiu-ency and he says, I have) got a work for the constituency. He wants foremen, and he says to his party friends, I am going to put you in as foreman, and I am going to get this other man employed in some other capacity. And so he selects the workers, all party men. He says to this foreman. We have to have so many cords of stone. He goes around amongst those who have supported him and whom he expects to support him again, and he says: All you who have stone, here is a chance to bring it in. From the moment you start to the moment you finish is it not a complete electioneering arrangement? The men who sell the stone are the recipients of what my hon. friend denominates the bounty of the government^-he remembers that phrase. They are told that the bounty of the government is being shared by virtue of the good will of the member whom they have elected, and whom they will be asked to elect again. From first to end, the work is confined to the party, is used to buttress up the members or the defeated candidate, and in all these things added expense is incurred. Here is an, example. Word goes out even when a contract is taken on. The contractor is informed that he must buy his lumber or stone within the constituency in which the work is situated. Instruction goes out from somebody. If it does not, what is the meaning of this letter?

Ottawa, February 10, 1908.
E. D. Lafleur, Esq.,
Chief Engineer,
Department of Publio Works,
City.
Dear sir,-With reference to our timber required for St. Alphonse work, Chicoutimi county, we find that to comply with the request of the member, Mr. Girard, to purchase all our timber in his constituency, we would have to take round timber from 12 inches up, as it is impossible to get 14 inch. We are very anxious to purchase everything in the constituency, and we trust that we will be allowed to take the round timber from 12 inches up to comply with the wishes of the member.
There may be no printed instructions sent to these men, but it works out; the member has it understood with the minister and knows exactly what his rights are and will insist on them and in the province of Quebec or in any other province he insists on his right and so the freedom of contract, the freedom of purchase, the freedom of wage, the freedom of the work from the beginning to the end is restricted by the party interests and the party advantages and the party privilege. That is not a way in which the country should do its business. I know that the Minister of Public Works believes that to be the case. But I never knew a proposition to be mentioned in this House in the way of criticism, affecting the minister's department, that he had not a defence for it. Why he even not very long ago

I want no better defence than the course pursued by the hon. gentleman when he had a chance.
Mr. FOSTER, -set up the defence that
if there was a candidate running in the interest of the government it was a proper thing that he should interest himself in peddling post office sites just previous to the time of election. The minister knows in his heart that that is not a correct system. His answer will be: You did the same thing. He has that in the back of his head now; I see it coming out, even before it receives audible expression.
And from one so perfect as my hon. friend it must have been correct.

There is another nice little phase of my hon. friend. When he is in a bad corner and his conscience troubles him a little-what he has left of it, and I hope he has a lot-he wants to say something about the virtues or perfection of the hon. member for North Toronto.
There is no harm in that.

But the nice little way in which he does it, as if he was to say: Oh,
good Lord, you know I am sinful and weak and will reserve a large lot of favour for me; but you know that the hon. member for North Toronto is all straight, do not give him an inch of liberty. My hon. friend knows that this is a bad business system. Will he not acknowledge that?

There is perhaps a little bit of human nature in my soul, and when I try to measure up as to whether my conduct is absolutely right or reasonably right,
I look to what other people have done who are at least as good as I am and who sometimes are thought by their friends and even by themselves to be a little better.

That is another nice little
thing.
How does that strike my hon. friend?
You mean the Minister of Agriculture?

As a new Minister of Public Works it certainly is not at all out of place in determining the course to be pursued by my department to look back and see what has been the course pursued for many years, even ever since confederation, and it certainly would not be out of place for me to ask the course pursued when my hon. friend had charge of the public affairs of this country to a very large degree, while occupying the very responsible position of Minister of Finance, and, apart altogether from that portfolio, when he filled a large place in the public affairs of this country. I did not and do not think it out of place for me to refer to the fact that during all the time he was in power and was a very important factor in the government of the country, the very same course was pursued that we are pursuing to-day. We ought to be reasonable about these things. I am satisfied that one of the things which has hurt my hon. friend as much as anything else in the opinion of the people of this country is that he pretends, if he will pardon me for saying it in a public way, that if he had the power he would pursue a different course politically from what he did when he was in power. When my hon. friend was in power his government and the Minister of Public Works in his government allowed the very thing to be done which is being done today. What is more reasonable than that the resident engineer, who has the carrying on of these small works in regard to which tenders are not called, which are not large enough to require calling for tenders, should be told to confer with the member for the county who is supposed to be certainly as intelligent as anybody else in the county, and whose interest it is to avoid any possibility of scandal and to see that the public work is done in the most economical manner possible?

Roche & Carney, for instance, in Halifax?
_ Mr. PUGSLEY. And whose interest it is to see that the most capable foreman is chosen and that the material going into the public works is bought at the lowest possible price. I think it is not unreasonable that the member supporting the government should be consulted. My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor), who is opposing the government, complained bitterly yesterday that I did not consult him and would not appoint a foreman whom he recommended. That hon. gentleman takes even a stronger view as to what should be done as to consulting representatives than we do on this side.
If you consult the member in one county it would be a good rule to apply in another county.

I shall explain the difference. The member supporting the government is interested in seeing that government work is carried on in a thoroughly honest and proper manner. Without any disrespect to hon. gentlemen opposite, I am not able to say that they have any such interest as that. I have seen my hon. friends' faces beam with joy when they discovered that there had been any apparent maladministration of public affairs on the part of even the smallest official in the employ of the government. Therefore, I think it is only right, if we are to confer with anybody, that our resident engineer should confer with those whose desire it is, in the public interest, to see that the works are carried on in a proper and economical way.
In case the member representing the county is opposed to the government to whom does the resident engineer go?

Then the resident engineer is instructed-we may as well be perfectly frank about it-to confer as a rule with the gentleman who had run as a candidate in support of the government. That _ has always been the practice, and that is the practice to-day; there is no use being hypocritical about these things; that is the way in which they are done.
Then you have not abolished the patronage system in your department?

Not so far as consulting for the selection of a foreman. We have the safeguard that even after the foreman is suggested by the member, the engineer is instructed not to employ him unless in his judgment he is a man who thoroughly understands the work and can '

be relied upon to perform his duties. As to the labouring men, they are, as a rule, employed by the foreman who is given a free hand. It is difficult often to get labouring men, and I happen to know that labourers on both sides of politics are chosen. As to the pay-sheets, the foreman is obliged to swear to their correctness, and when this sworn return is certified to by the resident engineer it comes to the chief engineer. The instructions to the resident engineer are of a very peremptory character to purchase materials only at the market rates, and as to whether he confers with friends of the government I have no knowledge. His duty is to see that the prices of material are fair and reasonable. The chief engineer has a pretty accurate knowledge of what are fair and reasonable prices for materials in all sections of the country, and he has to certify to the correctness of the bills, which then have to go to the chief accountant of the department, who must also be satisfied they are correct, and then to the Auditor General whose duty it is to review them. I do not think the hon. gentleman has presented any strong argument against the existing practice.
When the vote was taken last year it was promised the work would be completed, but only half the appropriation was spent.

As my hon. friend knows -and I hope he may not be annoyed at my referring to it because it might suggest a hint that he and his friends were responsible for it-we did not get the Supply Bill through until the middle of July, and the summer was more than half gone when we were able to commence the work.
Is it not a fact that in the case of pretty nearly every public work in Gaspe and Bonaventure the actual expenditure did not commence until about one month before the elections?
I do not think that can be true because we tried to get the work commenced as quickly as we could after parliament prorogued.

Will the minister have prepared a statement in respect to the expenditure in Gaspe and Bonaventure on harbours and rivers, showing at what date the several appropriations which were voted last parliament for these two counties commenced to be exipended? I mean the commencement of the expenditure, not in Ottawa, but on the works themselves.
I will be glad to get that.
I refer to the work done by day labour and not by contract.
All right.

The Minister of Public Works does not appear to have gTasped the force of the remarks I made to the House last night. Perhaps it was because it was so late at night and that we were all so tired with the arduous labours of the day that we were not in a position to grasp an idea so clearly as we could this afternoon.
Or to express it so clearly.

That may be. In order that there may be no misunderstanding on the subject I shall now endeavour to make clear what I stated to the committee last night, and in passing I would like to refer to a remark made now by the Minister of Public Works to the effect that he has no confidence in the honesty of gentlemen on this side of the House.
I did not surely go so far as that. I must have lost my head completely if I said that.
That is the second time to-day you lost your head.
Perhaps I said 'political' honesty.
Let us take it thai way.
I do not think I even went as far as that.

At all events I would direct the attention of the minister to the fact that while in investigations before committees of this House there have been brought out no facts reflecting on the political honesty of the Conservative members, there have been brought out very material facts reflecting upon the honesty, political and otherwise-
Order.

Let these hon. gentlemen opposite possess their souls in patience-reflecting upon the honesty, political and otherwise, of the gentlemen outside of this House to whom the Minister of Public Works has chosen to go for that advice which he might better have sought from the chosen representatives of the people. It was no member of the Conservative party who was concerned-only to mention one of the most glaring transactions brought to light-in the five cents a yard additional on the St. John dredging contract. The point I sought to make last night was that when the minister seeks for advice throughout this country as to the men to be employed, as to the persons from whom supplies should be purchased, as to all the details of the administration of his department, there can be no objection of course to his going to any official
source because then he goes to the man who is receiving pay for rendering the service which the minister requires of him. It is not surprising to me that in connection with the constituency of New Westminster the Minister of Public Works does not ask my advice as to whom he shall employ, although perhaps if he did it might save him trouble on some occasions. But it is surprising to me to hear him lay down the principle that in the constituency of New Westminster he should choose as the source of the inspiration of his official acts not the duly elected member for the constituency, not the late member who should possess the confidence of the government in every respect, but a man whose distinction is that he was rejected by the people by the largest majority they have ever given in an election. Here I give a concrete case of how this svstem works out, and one can speak more to the point in citing a concrete case than in dealing with generalities. The Minister of Public Works tells us he will continue this system in the face of the most solemn report of his own commissioners that the evil of the public life of this country has its origin in the patronage list. Notwithstanding the warning he has received from high official sources the Minister of Public Works has to-day declared it is his intention to perpetuate that evil and in each electoral district of this country enable some chosen instrument of his party to tithe all the contractors and to tithe all the employees in the service of the government; to make them contribute to a party political fund by the power he gives his instruments of having the final word as to who shall get this work, as to who shall be favoured with purchases by the government, and as to who shall be promoted to positions. I declare that system to be an abominable, one. In our part of the world-and other members can speak for their own districts-it has led to the most grave abuses. It has led to the contractors under the government and to the employees of the government being called upon for contributions of all kinds for purely party political work, and which contributions they are forced to make good at the expense of the people of Canada. That is the point I sought to make in the nro-test I registered here last night. That is the point which is bound to be discussed this session in view of the public announcement of the minister, and of other matters which have come to the knowledge of members of this House.

Thadee Desbiens.

Since the contract was awarded have any changes been made which lessen the quantity of the work to be done?
On the 29th of June there was a changei in location which added $2,955 to the contract, making the total contract $55,455.
Is it not a fact that the change made the wharf a hundred feet shorter?
I am not aware of that. Does my hon. friend state that? If so, I will have it looked into.
I am so informed. Where is the dredging being done-in the immediate vicinity of the wharf?
In front of the wharf, in the basin of the Chicoutimi harbour.
What depth of water does the minister wish to secure in front of the wharf?
Fifteen feet.
Is he aware that the dredge is working to a depth of 25 feet ?
I have heard that stated, but I have not been able to verify it.
Can the minister state what the dredge is doing with the soil that is being dug up opposite the wharf?
It is taken down to a part of the river where the water is deeper.
That is in the contract?
Yes.
And the contractor is under contract to do that with all the soil he digs out?
To deposit it wherever the resident engineer may direct. That is the usual specification.
If the resident engineer should direct it to be deposited at a point which would save the contractor an enormous sum of money, would the department feel interested in the matter?

That would depend entirely on circumstances. The department would not permit it to be deposited where it would interfere with navigation; but if it could be deposited in another place with equal advantage to the department without interfering with navigation, and the resident engineer allowed that to be done, I do not suppose the department would object.

If after a contract has been let, under the condition that the soil shall be deposited at a distant point, the contractor finds a place near by where it can be deposited more conveniently, and the resident engineer allows him to deposit it there, is any allowance made?
The dredged material has to be deposited at such place as the engineer in charge may direct.
Then the engineer in charge has it in his power to make it possible for the dredging contractor to make either very little or a great deal of money?

If the engineer insisted upon the contract taking the spoil an un-

reasonable distance, the contractor could protest to the chief engineer. In dredging contracts, the specifications are all alike in this respect, that the contractors must deposit the spoil at a specified place or at such other place as the resident engineer may-direct; and therefore if there is a place nearer at hand, where it could be deposited without interfering with navigation, I should think the contractor would have that in mind, and would ask the resident engineer to allow him to deposit it there. But ordinarily that question does not arise.

I shall give the minister the information which has come to me and which will at least bear investigation as to its absolute veracity. There is at Chicoutimi a pier built at right angles with the south shore. It runs north and south. It was decided to very much enlarge the area, and in order to do so another pier is being built from the end at right angles, thus making a sort of L upside down. It is expected that at the far side of the L there will be a further construction, making three sides, the shore being the fourth, and that will be filled in and so make a solid wall. The contract was given to one Thad-dee Desbiens. Tenders were called for. A number of responsible parties tendered, all of whom asked a pretty high figure. But Mr. Desbiens, a hotel-keeper at Chicoutimi, put in his tender at a very low figure, $52,500, and when his tender was accepted it was said by the local people that at that price he could make no money. But at the same time there was a contract made by the government with the dredging construction company whereby the dredge 'Algonquin' was set at work in that neighborhood. Four or five miles down the river there is a shallow channel and the government have been dredging out the channel in order to get a total 15 feet in depth. Opposite the pier there is already a depth of 15 feet, but the dredge 'Algonquin', which had the contract for dredging, is located immediately opposite the wharf, and it dug to the depth of 25 feet. And all the spoil which the 'Algonquin' dredged out was quietly taken, with the permission of the resident engineer, and dumped behind the pier which Desbiens was building. That made it unnecessary for him to bring down any dump and made it possible for the dredging contractor to get all his spoil placed within a very few yards of the place where he was dredging. Both the dredging contractor and the wharf builder benefited, and had it not been for the complacency of the resident engineer, the wharf could not have been built at the price. The result is a lot of unnecessary dredging. The dredge should have been located where a channel is wanted. But located where it is, it has served a double purpose, that of enabling the contractor to
make some money and enabling the dredging company to increase their large profits.
The wharf is built by Mr. Desbiens at a very much lower price than the work is fairly worth.

The others cannot see how it was possible for him to make money at the price but now we see how it was possible. The local resident engineer was the arbiter of the whole matter. He said to the dredge-owner: Work opposite the wharf and deposit all your spoil behind Desbien's revetment.
The contractor is doing a good thing for himself and for the country as well.
But how about the other one who is digging down to 25 feet?

I am afraid my hon. friend relies too much upon rumours. He does not know himself that the contractor has gone to a depth of 25 leet. He does not know that he has gone actually below 15 feet. It is the duty of the) resident engineer to keep very careful track of the dredging and he ought not to pay for a single yard of dredging below the specified depth. Until my hon. friend is able to state that the dredging has gone to a depth of 25 feet, I would not feel bound to accept that statement. There is a tide there of If. feet, and you might have to dredge 25 feet or 30 feet to get 15 feet below low water. I have no information on the point and am surprised to hear the statement or rather the suggestion of my hon. friend. If I had any evidence, I would feel it my duty to make careful inquiry.

There is certain circumstantial evidence which supports the contention of my informant. The depth of water opposite the wharf has been recognized by all concerned as 32 feet and that was ample for any vessel expected there. But that dredge has been hard at work digging where there are 22 feet already and bringing up lots of mud, which would lead one to conclude that they were doing extra dredging for the purpose of accommodating the wharf contractor.
Clarke City, Seven Islands-wharf improvement, $4,600.

This is to pay the balance due on the contract to the Messrs. Clark. The contractors are the North Shore Power Railway and Navigation Company. A contract was entered into with them on the 4th of January, 1907 for this wharf at $29,990. This company, of which the Messrs. Clark own the controlling interest, has expended a very much larger amount on this work, but all the department agreed to pay was $29,990. The actual

expenditure made would run up to nearly $75,000. The Messrs. Clark have inaugurated works of very large proportions at Clarke city and expended considerably more than a million dollars. They employ a great many hands, and the government felt that, under ordinary circumstances, they would have been justified, in the public interest, in paying the whole cost of this work. But it was undertaken in the first place by the company, and a compromise was made that the government should pay only $29,990, and that is all we asked the committee to vote. This amount $4,600 is to pay the balance due them under the contract.
Has some dredging been done at Clark city close to the wharf?
I am not at the moment aware, but I think some dredging was done there.

This is one of the pieces of work that, I think, reflects less credit on the department than almost any other along that north shore. The minister did not tell us that, after the wharf was built and the mud was taken away from beside it, the greater portion of the wharf turned turtle, and a great deal of money had to be spent in taking down the old material and building up again. The wharf was built on a very soft, oozy mud flat. You could stick a pole down five or six inches anywhere.
Was not the wharf that turned over the company's wharf, built before the government took hold of the matter?

It was originally the company's wharf, but it was taken over by * the government and the government have had to make the damage good. The trouble seems to have been due to the foolishness of taking out this soft mud beside the wharf. The government took over a private enterprise, and the private enterprise was so handled that it became practically useless and cost many thousands of dollars to put it in shape again. And all this for one private company.
How much money has the government put into the whole thing?
Up to 30th November last the government had paid altogether $102,562.29.
Can the minister tell me the name of the insipector of the work from June 15 to September 15, 1907?
There was a Mr. Charles Sweeny at one time-I do not know whether at the time the hon. member refers to or not.

I see it stated in the Auditor General's Report that Mr. L. P. Girard was the inspector. I understand that Mr. Girard was paid $2.50 per day. I would ask the minister if he knows that Mr. Girard was a law student at the time?
There is a Mr. Girard who was on the engineering staff of the resident engineer, Mr. Michaud. He was at one time at Chicoutimi. He was engaged on this work in the summer for one or two summers.
A son of the member?
Yes.
Is it a fact that a young law student was put on as inspector of an important work like this?
My information is that he is an engineering student.
He is practising law in Chicoutimi now.
That must be another man, because Mr. GiraTd is on the engineering staff of the department under Mr. Michaud at the present time. He was at Chicoutimi at one time on Mr. Tache's staff.

It is important that we should know the facts [DOT] in this matter, in view of the statement made by the hon. member (Mr. Blondin) that this man who was appointed inspector was a law student. If the minister cannot state the facts definitely now, he can learn them and give them to us later-say when we meet at eight o'clock.

No, Mr. Tache, the resident engineer, would have to be communicated with. I will get the information as soon as possible. It should not be necessary to let the item stand. The amount is small and we should close up this matter.

The passing of this item is not important; we have a month or two to deal with it. The fact of nutting on a man as inspector who was not qualified may account for the loss. Of course, the present minister was not in charge, and may not be personally liable to censure. But someone in his department is. If we pass the item now, we shall never get the information. As far as I am concerned, I would like the item to stand, so that we may learn whether the statement made to the committee is correct or not. If the minister can show that this man was a competent inspector, of course, the item will pass.

When I explain the case to the hon. member (Mr. J. D Reid)

I	am confident he will not press his request. The wharf which, it is alleged, fell down, was not built by the government, but by the company. Since the government rebuilt it, it has stood perfectly.

That is not the point. What we want to know is whether it is the policy of the government to have incompetent men as inspectors of important works. The minister must know that this is not the only case in which unqualified men have been appointed as inspectors of important public works. If the minister had been here a few years ago and had stood with me at the corner of this building and seen the new tower of the western block fall, he would realize more clearly the importance of having good inspectors. I understand that the inspector who had the supervision of the work on this tower had never seen stonework or brickwork in progress before. It cost the country many thousands of dollars to make good that mistake. We find that on dredging works the government have men who are not competent. They put on men who are mere labourers at $1.50 or $2.50 a day, and the running of the whole thing is left to the contractor. If, in order to give a law student a holiday with pay the government have caused serious loss to the country, this committee should know it.

There is a little more in this than appears on the surface, and enough to make it necessary to discuss it for a few minutes at any rate. Here was a work of considerable difficulty, because the first wharf constructed there had collapsed, and it was found necessary to rebuild, removing the old wharf. The wharf was built on a very peculiar bottom, and consequently the construction required engineering management of considerable skill. Now what was done? A young man. who is the son, I understand, of the federal member, and who is a law student, was sent up there for his summer holidays. He got $2.50 a day while he stayed there, and all his expenses, as well as $116 for his board and travelling expenses. He spent a very pleasant vacation in the neighbourhood, and came back again, having had his whole summer at the expense of the government. He resumed the study of law, and has I believe just been admitted to the bar.
If the facts are as the hon. gentleman alleges, I will get the information about it as soon as I reasonably can.

Let the item stand in the meantime.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Last session preliminary steps were taken by the government to build a railway to Hudson bay and surveyors have been put in the field at considerable expense to the country. The map exhibited in the Railway Committee shows this line cutting through what is supposed to be the government line, which apparently runs to Fort Churchill while this line apparently is projected to reach Fort Nelson. It is stated that Mr. Armstrong, government engineer, has reported in effect that a suitable harbour cannot be obtained at Fort Churchill, and that while Fort Nelson harbour was none too good it can be made suitable by a considerable expenditure. We have had a flood of oratory if not of reason within the last few days about the desirability of free trade in railways, but we have also had the matured wisdom of several members of the government in earlier days impelling them to point out the inadvisability of multiplying railways in suoh. a way that they may become an increased charge on the people. Every sane statesman recognizes that if you construct two lines of railway where there is only business for one, the charge in the end must fall on _ the people. There may be infinite possibilities for railway development in the direction of Hudson bay, but at present it is in the experimental stage, and if the country is to build a railway to Hudson bay there is no reason why we should encourage a competing line. We extended the Transcontinental Railway to Moncton and we were told by the government that we were forced into that position by the stupidity of the Tones in building the Intercolonial on its present location. The Minister of Railways has now a chance to prevent anything of that kind occurring in the future; he has the ! ball at his foot and I hope he will do the kicking on this occasion and see that these people do not get this charter if it is going to injuriously affect the government road. I see there is another charter sought for a railway to Hudson bay in addition to this one, and as the object of the government in building a line is to find a short route for our western grain to Liverpool, and not for the purpose of developing local traffic, it makes no difference whether these lines parallel each other or not, for so long as their destination is a port on the Hudson



bay they must be in competition. The minister did not refer to this matter in the Railway Committee.

speechtext: It is hard to get a word in there.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: That is true, but I trust the hon. gentleman will now say there is a good deal of reason why we should hesitate to incorporate railway companies into that country at present. If the minister thinks it is all right I will not make a very big kick, but I hope it will not result in our having to buy out these charters as has been our experience in the past.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: The giving of a large number of charters over any particular territory does not mean that there will be a large number of railways in that territory. The difficulty in Canada is, and I suppose it is not peculiar to us, that the number of railways constructed is small in proportion to the number of charters granted. As to the building of more than one railway through any particular territory, my hon. friend's observations may in some cases be correct, but generally speaking it is against the well established usage of Bndeavouring to get competition in railway lines. If two stores exist where there would be only a good living for one, the argument of the hon. gentleman is that the people would pay more for their goods because the two stores would have to be maintained, and while he is right in theory he is wrong in practice, because competition would compel them to sell their goods lower so as to allow one of them at all events to live, and in the end it would be the survival of the fittest. Mr. Armstrong is an engineer sent out by the government to survey the route from Pas Mission to Fort Churchill, and if I remember correctly, his report is not that Fort Churchill would not provide a suitable harbour but that he has been given information which leads him to believe that Nelson might provide a better harbour. There is a greater difference of opinion on that point than I had thought existed until I read this report. It is only to-day I had a conversation with a man well known in Canada who made an exploration through that part of the country some years ago on behalf of the then Ontario government' and he is confident that Nelson is the better harbour of the two.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: That coincides with Armstrong.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: Yes, but it is fair to say that Mr. Armstrong says his report is only based on information he had received. I may say frankly that it is my intention to have Mr. Armstrong survey the route to Nelson as well as to Churchill so that we may have information obtained from an actual survey, and I have an item

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: in the estimates to pay for that-. I think it would be wise to take what he has reported even if it is only hearsay information. The route to be taken by these roads is not the route of the government line. The government line starts at The Pas, and runs to Churchill or Nelson as the case may be. If it runs to Churchill, the distance is 497 miles. This road starts in the vicinity of Prince Albert, runs south to a certain point further east than our line, and then to Churchill. I am not sure that it would be wise to prevent these charters being granted, because I am a bit skeptical as to the number of railways that will be built to Hudson bay. My own opinion is that the country will be glad, and I shall be satisfied, if one railway is constructed at an early day. But I am not prepared to say that we ought not to grant a charter or two for a line to run from Prince Albert in the direction I have indicated, even if we should build a line of our own to Hudson bay. I may say to the committee that there was strong pressure brought to bear on the government to start our line from Prince Albert; a deputation waited upon the Minister of Railways and urged that view. I pointed out that they already had a charter for a line from Prince Albert, that that line was surveyed or would be surveyed, and that our idea was to give the most direct connection from the railways now in existence to Hudson bay. Conditions vary so much in different parts of the country that it is impossible to lay down a hard and fast rule as to railway charters. Under some conditions it is wise to give as many charters as are wanted in order to get a railway built, because there is the danger of refusing a charter to the people most apt to build it. There are circumstances when it would he unwise to grant new charters, as they might possibly injure a business enterprise about to be launched. We have to deal with the different projects on their merits. Personally I see no objection to giving charters for a dozen lines to Hudson bay.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext:
It is true that if you have two grocery stores on opposite corners, the prices of goods may be reduced by competition; but our railway board is not working in that way. We have established it at considerable expense, which is likely to increase as the years go by, and the theory on which it is based is this, that it shall see that the tariffs of the railways are so adjusted that they shall have a reasonable return on capital, working expenses, and _ so on, and that consistently with that object the rates shall be reduced to the people as much as possible. So that the minister's argument in that respect does not apply to this case. It is exactly the opposite, if our railway board does its duty, as I expect it will. If you put two roads where there is only a legitimate

amount of traffic for one, the railway board, when it comes to adjust the rates, will have to allow such rates as will pay ordinary working expenses and a reasonable return on the capital invested. If one railway can serve the needs of that country for the time being, and the government, as I assume, are going to build a railway, and you have another railway built to serve the same purpose, whether it is exactly parallel or not, you will diminish the profits of both roads, and each will have to charge the traffic a larger amount than it would otherwise do. The minister mentioned that the government were urged to start their road from Prince Albert. That is a very effective answer to the argument which we have often heard in the Railway Committee and sometimes in this House, that we do not interfere with freedom of action by granting a charter. The minister says tHat by reason of the fact that there was already a charter granted for a line from Prince Albert, he decided that the government would not begin their railway from that point.

speechtext:
I did not quite say that.
I stated as a fact that there was a charter for a road from Prince Albert, and that it was the object of the government to get the closest connection from the existing railways to the Hudson bay.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: As I undersood, the minister was influenced by that fact, as a wise minister would be, because he would not want to build a railway over the same line for which there was already a charter. Where, as the minister himself suggests, one railway would probably serve the purpose completely for the present, we are not acting in the interest of the people or with good judgment if we grant this charter while we are contemplating building a road ourselves.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I have a letter in my hand from a gentleman of the name of Mr. Green. It is dated Fort Churchill, and I received it to-day. He gives some information in regard to this matter which I think it might not be out of place to state to the House. He has been there all summer. I saw him in Prince Albert before he left, and he told me that when he reached Fort Churchill he would send me a letter. I would point out to the House that Prince Albert bears very much the same relation to Hudson bay that Winnipeg does to Fort William. There was _ a time when people thought that_ one railway from Winnipeg to Fort William would be quite sufficient, but we shall very soon have three, and one of them will be double tracked. We need have no feaT whatever in granting charters for railways to Hudson bay. Hudson bay must ultimately be the outlet for the northern parts of both
801	:1 I ii '
Saskatchewan and Alberta, and no doubt before many years we shall see a railway running from Edmonton to Athabasca lake and thence to Depot harbour on Chesterfield inlet; another from Prince Albert to Fort Churchill, and probably another running east of Lake Winnipeg to York Factory. The probability is that York Factory is the best harbour, but Fort Churchill from what I have heard can be made an exceedingly good harbour, and it is considerably nearer to Europe. We will need all these harbours. Of course the traffic will require to go through Hudson straits after leaving Fort Churchill. It is considerably nearer to Europe than Port Nelson. It is not fair to the northern part of Saskatchewan and Alberta to ask them to send their trade away round to Nelson, nearly 150 miles out of the way from Prince Albert. There are settlers seventy-five miles north of Prince Albert and you ask them to send their produce to Prince Albert, then across the Northern Saskatchewan and then afterwards the southern Saskatchewan, and then go way down out of their way in a circle and come back to the crossing of those rivers at La Pau. From all I can hear there are no great difficulties to be encountered between the north part of Prince Albert and Fort Churchill. My correspondent tells me that there are great mistakes being made in locating railways in that country. In some places the moss between Split lake and Port Nelson is so exceedingly thick that it acts as a cover for the frost, just like straw in an ice-house, and prevents the ground from thawing out in the summer. But when a Tailway shall be constructed and this moss disturbed and gathered up the heat of the sun will penetrate into the ground and very often the bottom will be very apt to go out of the railway. More than that, my correspondent tells me that from Split lake to Port Nelson a great deal of the ground is simply muskeg. It would appear, therefore, to be almost impossible to continue the road the government have had surveyed from La Pau by way of Split lake to Fort Churchill, and it will be necessary to go to Port Nelson some other way. I see no reason why we should not have three or four railways, and even at my age I hope to live to see the day when there will be a double tracked railway running from Prince Albert to Fort Churchill. The government need have no fear to grant a charter. If we get plenty of charters, no doubt some of the companies chartered will undertake to build.
There is another thing. A few days ago the Minister of Railways, in answer to a question I put him, told us that the Nelson river might in time become navigable. If that be the case, why should not the two Saskatchewan rivers also become navig-

able? We all know that the difficulty in these rivers is that they're full of shifting sand. The sand bars form so rapidly that it is difficult to continue navigation. There is an item of $21,000 to clear the boulders out of the northern Saskatchewan this year which means that it is expected to make ft navigable. No doubt if we do not have navigation on these rivers, we will have two canals, one from Edmonton to Prince Albert, and the other following the course of the south Saskatchewan, and then we may expect that Prince Albert will grow to be a great deal larger than Winnipeg. The grain will be transhipped from these canals to the railway from Prince Albert to Fort Churchill. I desire also to draw attention to the fact that there is no doubt that Hudson bay is open for as long a period in the year, or nearly as long as Lake Superior. We must not forget that Lake Superior is frozen up for a great part of the year. And, from what I have read in history, and from what I know of Hudson bay, I am led to believe that the season of navigation there is as long as that on Lake Superior. I made reference before to the situation of Winnipeg in relation to Lake Superior being similar to that of Prince Albert in relation to Hudson bay. In 1811, we find, Lord Selkirk came into Hudson bay with old Edward and Anne,' an old worn out ship, and with another ship that was no better, and brought in his settlers, landing them at York Factory. At that time, there were no lighthouses, no wireless telegraphy-none of the advantages and aids to navigation that can easily be pro-vjded now. If we had lighthouses, signal stations and wireless telegraphy, I have no doubt that it would be quite possible to navigate Hudson bay for several months longer every year than at the present time. We know that the ice drifts south from Fury_ and Hecla ^straits and Fox channel, and if it comes in that direction, it must be driven to the south of Hudson strait. That being so, there must be open water near the northern shore of Hudson strait, even at a season when that strait is now supposed to be blocked with ice. With modern facilities, there can be no reasonable doubt, Hudson bay will be open to navigation for as many days of the year as Lake Superior is. I do not think that we should hesitate to grant all the charters that are required.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Before that order is passed, I would like to get an expression from the minister on a very important point. It is stated by the government that the matter of assisting the railways to Hudson bay is under consideration and that money will be voted for the purpose of bonusing or building the road. I would like to have a statement from the Minister Mr. THOS. CHISHOLM.
of Railways on this point. If these charters are granted and the government should undertake to build a railway itself or assist a railway such as the Grand Trunk Pacific, will it undertake to compensate the holders of these charters for any expenditure they may have made or claim to have made while they were holding their charters. The moment the government steps in and proposes; to bonus one of the companies holding a charter, the others will make a claim for compensation. It would be well for the minister to announce that there will be no compensation whatever in such a case. He will recollect many occasions when claims, in similar circumstances, were made for compensation by the holders of charters who never did anything with them. If we are going to give free trade in charters, which virtually is the policy of the railway committee, there should be a declaration by the government that any expenditure made by the holders of these charters, unless they proceed to build the road, will not be considered in fixing any compensation when the matter of bonuses comes up or the matter of building a railway.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: We are glad to grant these companies a privilege, and undertaking no obligation towards them whatever I could understand the situation when it would be fair that some compensation should be given a company holding a charter if this were the situation. Suppose a company had surveyed a certain route and the government stepped in and proposed to build on that route, it would be but right to compensate the company for the money it had spent in laying out that line. But except in such a case, the government has no intention whatever of giving any compensation.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: I think that the government and parliament will have to be more careful in future in granting railway charters. It is only fair that great corporations, engaged in railway construction, should be treated generously by the government, but where promoters secure charters for other purposes than constructing the road, the government should be more careful. It is only fair that the government should state whether any of these gentlemen who are the provisional directors and who are not well known in Canada as railway constructors are bona fide railway men. Either the minister or the promoter of the Bill should be in a position to state this. They should be able to state whether there is any hope of the road being constructed under these directors or whether this charter is being obtained for the purpose of selling it to some other company.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: I have absolutely no personal interest in this Bill. I take charge of it because I believe the charter asked for is one that ought to be granted by this House. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) wants to know if the men whose names appear as provisional directors are, bona fide, seeking this charter for the purpose of building the road or seek it merely for speculative purposes. So far as I know, their intention is to build the road-not all of it right away, but a part of it. A part of this road is urgently needed at this time. From the city of Prince Albert north, east and west some sixty or seventy miles, there is a tract of country a considerable part of which is good farming laud, and some of which is very fine timber country. Settlers are loath to go into that district because there is no railway accommodation. Therefore, the first sixty or seventy miles of this road would be in the nature of a colonization road. As the committee are aware, the local government of Saskatchewan is assisting branch lines and colonization roads to a very considerable extent, and the promoters of this company have every reason to believe that, as soon as they are prepared to go on with the work, they will be able to secure aid from the provincial government. So, I think I can assure my hon. friend that the charter is being asked for in good faith, for the purpose of building the railway. While I am on my feet, I may say that it rather surprised me to hear the remarks of the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). Surely he is not aware of the condition of affairs in western Canada, or he would not state that one road to Hudson bay should and would meet the needs of western Canada.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: The minister says that one railway will be enough at present.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: One railway may be enough by way of experiment-and we know that the value of the road to Hudson bay is somewhat experimental. But the people of western Canada believe that it is a feasible route and that, at no very distant day, a large part of the produce of western Canadian farms will be shipped by way of Hudson bay. Should that prove to be the case, the hon. gentleman, of course, will not ask us to believe that one railroad will be sufficient to carry the produce of our western Canadian prairies to the markets of the world. So far as the route of this road is concerned, it does not interfere, as I understand the matter, with the railway projected by the government. I was pleased to hear the remarks of the hon. member for East Huron (Mr. Chisholm) in relation to granting this and similar charters to Hudson bay, and I hope that, in the interests of the people who wish to settle in the country north of Prince Albert, and in the interest of all western Canada, this charter will be granted.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: I ana sorry to have to disagree with my hon. friend from South Simcoe because I do not think the people of Canada care how many railroads run parallel to each other, provided they are built at the expense of the corporations who receive these charters. I do not see where any danger arises in this case. If this road were to be built right away, these people, of course, would never obtain any subsidies from the government. Except in the case of railways, which, to reach from point to point must go through some narrow pass which will not accommodate more than one road, I do not see why the government should exercise great care in giving charters as my hon. friend wants them to do. Where there is room for many roads, parliament may well charter these roads, to be built at the expense of those who receive the charter. Judging from the way the government have treated the province of Ontario in not subsidizing the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway, we may believe that the government will leave these other people to build the roads at their own expense.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: I want to make it plain that I do not oppose railways, but I want the people to have them on reasonable terms, that is, I want the government to do what is right. The government should either occupy this field or else give it up to others to occupy. If they are going to occupy that field, they should see that they serve it properly. We should not have the same thing happening that we had in reference to the Intercolonial, and after these roads are built be asked to buy the roads out. Would it not be better for the government to adopt a definite policy now and say:	We will occupy that territory and serve it; or else get out of the field and let an ordinary company in.

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext: What policy would my hon. friend adopt, that the government should take hold, or get out and give it to a company?

subsubtopic: PRINCE ALBERT AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY.
speechtext:
When I occupy the place the hon. gentleman occupies, I will have a policy, and when that time comes I won't be afraid to tell the people what my policy is. When I occupy a position of that kind ,1 will say:	'Gentlemen, we are going in
there and we are going to occupy that field, but we will occupy it on terms profitable to the people that we represent as the government of Canada, and profitable to the people whom we are to serve in that region. We will have our feeders running into our trunk lines, and it will be a profitable enterprise.' But on the other hand, what the government are doing is this, they are going to build their railway, they are going to) let others build feeders from Prince Albert and Port Nelson; we will have the lean

part of it, and the others will have the rich part, and we will pay for both.

Before we resume consideration of item 143 I would like to mention a matter for the information of my hon. friend the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). I am inclined to think that both he and I, when we spoke this afternoon, were acting upon a wrong interpretation which we had taken from the answer vhich I had given to the House, I was misled, and I think he was misled also, by the amount which was in the estimates when that matter was under consideration before the committee a few days ago. The amount printed in the estimates was $57,000; the amount which had been asked for by the chief architect was $37,000. My hon. friend knows that the figure 5 and the figure 3 very often look alike upon the carbon copy of typewritten paper. The amount should be $37,000 instead of $57,000. So the answer which was given by me on the 10th instant, and which appears upon page 2391 of ' Hansard,' was that the estimated cost of $96,000 covered the cost of the building, heating, fittings of all kinds and all those expenses which are set forth upon the same page. As a matter of fact, the information of the chief architect is that the total cost will be something under that, and may not exceed $94,000. I am very glad to be able to give that information to the committee. My hon. friend can look up the figures, and if he takes the memorandum which I gave and substitute $37,000 for $57,000, he will see how the error has occurred. I have no doubt he was misled by these figures, as I was myself. When we come finally to pass the item I will have the correction made. I regret that the error occurred, and I am very sorry if it was the means of causing any
misunderstanding between my hon. friend and myself.
What was the number of the item?

It is in Ontario Public Biddings, item 132, Kingston Royal Military College, additional accommodation. $55,000 was voted last year, and $37,000 will entirely complete the building, and provide for heating, electric wiring, furnishing and fittings of all kinds.

I am glad to hear the explanation given by the minister. I was seeking to ascertain where that money went. It seems to me the minister's explanation justifies the stand I took in endeavouring to find out. We discussed the item on the basis of $57,000 and on a total of $112,000, and dividing the $112,000 by 16 cottages we found that the total cost for each cottage was 7,000.
Of course if the item had been going through at $37,000 it would not have been necessary for me to ask so many questions.
Mr- PUGSLEY. What puzzled me was seeing the item at $57,000, and I had the memorandum of the chief architect that the total cost was $96,000. I am very glad I have been able to set the item right.
